items.title: 30 Years Later, One of the Greatest ‘X-Files’ Episodes is Still a Misunderstood Masterpiece
items.summary: For the first three seasons of The X-Files , the writers kept you guessing, not only with regard to the show’s greater mysteries about aliens, but also about its most intriguing character. The Cigarette Smoking Man , played by William B. Davis, begins the series as a shadowy, silent character in the first episode. He looks on as Agent Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson) is given her not-too-subtle orders to undermine Agent Fox Mulder (David Duchovny) and his work on the X-Files. He goes on to appear sparingly, just a few times each season, to stop Mulder and Scully from getting too close to the secrets he’s spent decades covering up.

For starters, the NHS is urging players to “try and take regular breaks.” This helps avoid eye strain, and getting up from your gaming chair or sofa every couple of hours is good for circulation, relieving muscle stiffness, and providing mental clarity. The NHS’s post was particularly concerned with RSI, or repetitive strain injury, which it described as “pain that can be caused by repeated movement of part of the body, such as hands and fingers.”

items.title: Blizzard Tries 2 World of Warcraft Dungeon Fixes Over the Weekend to Stop Boosting Services
items.summary:
World of Warcraft Forever has now been out for a couple of weeks, and it's had a remarkably smooth launch. But now that players are starting to level up enough to engage with dungeons, Blizzard is trying to nail down exactly how dungeons should reward players.

Over the weekend, Blizzard pushed out a November 13 hotfix that made it so if there's any player in a group that's too high of a level to earn experience from monsters, no one in that group gets experience. The goal seems to be to get rid of boosting, where one high-level player can carry a group of players through dungeons to level them up quickly. But that solution backfired.

The problem is that in a lot of Forever's dungeons, there's a wide level range, so players on the high end of that range ended up accidentally nullifying everyone else's experience in the dungeon. That even happened to me on Saturday when trying to run Excavation Site with a level 37 player in my group.

The next day, Blizzard admitted that hotfix went too far. On the WoW Forever forums, community manager Kaivax posted , saying, "Yesterday, we updated dungeon play so that experience granted by an enemy in an instance is nullified if a high level player is in the group and enemy is trivial to that player. For some dungeons, the new restriction missed the mark because of the overall level range of the enemies in the dungeon."

Instead, Blizzard changed the way the restriction works. Rather than basing it on whether or not an enemy is "trivial" to any of the players, there's now a flat level difference restriction on experience. As Kaivax puts…

A 2023 assessment found Kurtaj had "acute autism" and was determined to return to "cybercrime" as soon as possible, despite the fact that he was literally standing trial for doing cybercrimes. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. Call of Duty is an inherently conservative series. You know what you're getting: guns, explosions, cinematic flourishes inspired by action movies, and probably some jingoism. And that's largely what the annual series' adherents seem to want. But it could be so much more. 

Taylor Kurosaki, writer and co-director for Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare , tells us he still thinks it has broad potential. That's why Infinite Warfare was set in the future—though, at the time, the team didn't realise it would end up being the third futuristic CoD, following Advanced Warfare and Black Ops 3. 

"Look, Call of Duty is a massive tree with a lot of branches, right? It can be World War 2. The team at IW had prototyped a medieval Call of Duty. Where you were a knight and had a sword and all kinds of crazy shit. But if it's a war story, sure, it can be Call of Duty."

I would love for that to be true. Call of Duty: The American Revolutionary War, Call of Duty: The Hundred Years War, Call of Duty: Napoleon. A military romp that isn't set between 1941 and 2065. After 23 years, it would be nice to see it spread out a bit. 

But big swings are not in CoD's nature. Or rather, Activision isn't particularly interested in rocking the money boat. A medieval CoD isn't the only massive detour the series almost took. Before it was forced to salvage Infinity Ward's Modern Warfare 3, Sledgehammer was working on a third-person horror game set in Vietnam, called Call of Duty: Fog of War .

items.title: Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes
items.summary:
Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".
items.t: Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

items.title: Biostar announces the first Intel Panther Lake motherboard and it's tiny, but don't get your hopes up for cramming it into a mini gaming PC
items.summary:
Motherboard manufacturer Biostar has just announced the BIPTL-IHT, a mini motherboard complete with an integrated Panther Lake-H processor. It's the first desktop Panther Lake motherboard to be released in retail.

As spotted by VideoCardz , the motherboard range has support for up to 128 GB of DDR-7200 MHz SO-DIMM memory and can come with the following chips:

Intel Core Ultra 5 325 / 335 / 336H Intel Core Ultra 7 355 / 365/ 356H / 366H Intel Core Ultra 9 386H All of these chips come with Xe3 graphics with four Xe cores, and are lacking the punchy integrated B390 iGPU (and its 12 Xe3 cores) that some mobile Panther Lake chips have. You can still do some light gaming on these integrated graphics, but you won't be making yourself a mini gaming PC with Biostar's latest. 

Instead, it seems like the purpose of this motherboard is to support industrial PCs, but given Xe3 graphics support hardware-accelerated AV1 encoding and decoding, one could feasibly use the motherboard in a mini media server PC instead. 

You are getting two M.2 Key-M slots here, with PCIe 5.0 x4 and PCIe 4.0 x2 connections. This allows for NVMe storage, and the memory is dual-channel too. You also get two HDMI ports, two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, and the motherboard can support up to four displays at once. 

As it's a 'Thin' Mini-ITX motherboard, its dimensions are 170 mm by 170 mm. That's very small. We don't yet have a release date or price point for this motherboard range. 

Still, it's a bit of a shame we don't have any mini motherboards with gaming-worthy integrated Panther Lake mobile chips yet.…
items.t: Biostar announces the first Intel Panther Lake motherboard and it's tiny, but don't get your hopes up for cramming it into a mini gaming PC

items.title: Final Fantasy 14 really wants Evercold to be the expansion everyone comes back to, so much so it's giving you 30 days free gametime if you've been gone long enough
items.summary:
Final Fantasy 14 is set to make some big changes when the upcoming expansion Evercold releases in February. An overhaul to combat, dailies, and new raid difficulties are set to shake things up and, hopefully, keep people sticking around for longer.

And judging by a recent Letter from the Producer , Naoki Yoshida really wants folks coming back to see what Evercold is all about. So much so that the game's offering 30 free days for long-gone adventurers… or a quick-and-dirty paid skip if you're so inclined.

"Encouraging players to return is no mean feat," Yoshida wrote. "People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons, including dissatisfaction and loss of interest. Although we continually update the game to address such issues, the fact remains that getting players to resume their journey is a difficult task indeed."

I can only assume that for that reason, the decision's been made to offer up a $9 cash shop item that'll skip you through Endwalker's patch story, as well as all of Dawntrail up until the final story patch. Now Final Fantasy 14 has offered paid story skips in the past—it still does—but this is the first time it's explicitly offered one for the current expansion. Usually the skips'll stop dead before the current expansion, meaning you still need to play through the newest story.

(Image credit: Square Enix) It's a pretty niche paid skip, too. You'll need to have at least completed Endwalker's main story and have a level 90 job on your chosen character, and even then you'll still have to level up to 100 in your own time in order to tackle the final patch…

items.title: World of Warcraft: Forever player turns their paladin into a near-unkillable healbot, solos a level 60 monster at level 30, and swims into the ocean
items.summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever's having some teething issues with its new spellcaster itemisation. The idea, to sum it up quick, is that a lot of the power that was in spells innately has been pushed onto items, instead, with the intention to make it feel really good when you get a cool new staff as a mage, for instance. 

This has had unintended consequences, as discovered by Rextroy (the same madlad who solos raid bosses ), as shared on YouTube . The problem is this: Gear in Forever can give a lot of raw power to your healing and damage spells, as part of the aforementioned changes. But that raw power also applies to lower-level healing spells, too.

In Forever (and in Classic), casting lower-level spells is a core part of managing your mana as a healer. In this instance, however, "the healing coefficient on healing power remains the same, which is around 43% [on a low level Flash of Light], so if I stack all healing green items, I get my healing power up towards 242," Rextroy explains.

This, combined with the Paladin talent Oath of Light (which slaps another 61 healing onto Flash of Light), along with Spiritual Focus and Concentration Aura, which makes it almost impossible for enemies to interrupt or push-back the casting of his Flash of Light, and this makes his paladin basically unkillable.

The low-rank version of his Flash of Light spell doesn't cost enough mana to outpace his natural mana regeneration, it heals for a bunch because of his gear, and enemies can't slow or interrupt it. Which makes him almost unkillable.

Ashes of the Singularity 2 can't be faulted for scale. Much like its predecessor, the RTS sequel delivers on the promise of letting players control truly colossal armies. Rolling up huge globs of units and tossing them at your enemy lines in a giant, explosion-riddled mud fight is never subtle and only occasionally clever. But for any veteran RTS player, watching miles-long lines of armies clash is inevitably going to stir the soul.

Unfortunately, scale is also the sum of what Ashes of the Singularity 2 offers. As a sequel, it does little to build on the strengths of the original, while largely failing to address that first game's weaknesses. The campaign is terrible, the story borderline incomprehensible, and the whole experience is overshadowed by the spectre of generative AI.

items.title: 'Game dev isn't always straightforward': Overwatch's director responds to players upset about season 6's hero being a DPS
items.summary:
Last week we found out a few new things about the next hero coming to Overwatch in season 6. He's an omnic detective, his name's Hudson , he has a fun accent, and he will be a DPS. Hudson is the last hero to be released from the batch teased earlier this year during Overwatch's Spotlight , and after all this time I'm very excited to see what he has to offer. But not everyone shares this sentiment. 

There's a good chunk of players who are upset about Hudson, before they've even tried him out, simply because he's not a support hero, which was what Team 4 initially promised him to be. I've seen this discontent online and honestly ignored it, thinking it was either bots or people farming for attention because I cannot fathom why anyone is honestly upset about this. 

(Image credit: Blizzard Entertainment) I've been maining support in Overwatch for almost 10 years now, ever since open queue grinded me down and I accepted that no matter how much I liked DPS, I had to role fill if we wanted to win games. So, after all these years I love getting my hands on a new support hero, but after four new supports this year (including Sombra's transition to the role), I'm more than satisfied with the role's current diversity of heroes. 

But Team 4 is taking the criticism seriously, as Keller has addressed it directly. Aside from trying to convince players that shoehorning a hero into a role just because that was the plan 10 months ago isn't a great idea, he also explains how "game dev isn't always straightforward" and how the team needs "to adapt to create the best version of something".…

items.title: Intel hit with class action alleging it 'misled investors' – company's recent downturn due in part to how darn expensive PCs are right now
items.summary:
Hot on the heels of a monumental share price drop for the company, Intel now faces a class action lawsuit from its own shareholders. 

This is according to an alert from law firm Robbins LLP , which recently informed all investors. This suit alleges "Intel misled investors about demand for its products and the Company's future growth potential."

The class action can involve anyone who bought stock between July 23, 2026, and October 29, 2026, known as the "class period".

With the memory crisis in full effect, PC sales are down worldwide ( estimated to be 20% down in October ), but the lawsuit argues that the PC sales slowdown was "having a materially greater negative impact to Intel’s third quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Group results than defendants had disclosed to investors."

It also argues Intel's OEM and distribution partners were left with hardware they couldn't sell to consumers due to rising prices, and that positive impacts of Intel business coming from the AI boom were off "more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup."

(Image credit: Intel) The suit also alleges that Intel's reporting of its operations and ability to capitalise on the AI boom "were materially false and misleading when made, and such statements did not accurately reflect Intel’s then-present business and prospects."

With Robbins LLP informing investors of this class action lawsuit, it's possible more could join the claim, and we don't actually know how many are…
items.t: Intel hit with class action alleging it 'misled investors' – company's recent downturn due in part to how darn expensive PCs are right now

items.title: New Asus beta BIOS patches now include a fresh AMD feature to stop you thinking your PC's b0rked
items.summary:
Memory training is boring stuff. Your PC will spend an age running through it when you first boot your PC, or you swap in some new RAM sticks (lucky you), or you make a change which has anything to do with memory in your BIOS. Or just because your PC decides it might fancy doing it again. But a new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta BIOS update, first from Asus (via Uniko's Hardware ), has made this whole process a lot more exciting.

Well, going from not at all exciting to something is always going to feel like a bigger deal, but I don't necessarily want to oversell it. Though when you're waiting for memory training to complete it's real nice to at least have a readout to indicate that it is progressing and your PC hasn't just hung.

This is the issue with memory training on PCs in the past. It was pretty damned opaque, in that you'd start up your PC and it would do… nothing. The fans would spin up, and the lights would light, but you'd have no readout on your monitor, and the debug screen on your motherboard would just have a static figure. Mine would be stuck on '15' for an age. 

Obviously you could just go looking up the error code and it would inform you that your system was just having a good long think about its system memory, but if you didn't know that could be a thing, it can feel like your rig is bricked.

The new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta patches are out now, first from Asus, but you can bet other motherboard vendors will be following suit soon enough. This latest version of the AGESA BIOS brings with it AMD's new memory training function, which shows on the motherboard's debug…

items.summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever 's been pretty great. At this point, I have around 150 hours played, a terrible posture problem, and a level 47 warrior I just barely avoided doing a 2 am Zul'Farrak run with yesterday. Speaking of, there has been a point of contention: Dungeons. 

My position on the debate is fairly neutral —I think you could maybe bump up the mob XP by around 10% as a compromise—but overall I think they're fine. The new ones are bangers, and I get a huge bunch of XP from doing them at least once. Blizzard's recent choices, however, did have me scratching my head over the weekend.

For a short time, via a hotfix , enemies in dungeons wouldn't give experience points to anyone in the group if they were trivial (that is, greyed out) to at least one party member. On paper, this sounds incredibly reasonable. WoW has suffered from a plague of dungeon boosters (that is, people selling runs of dungeons to let folks AFK through their levelling journey) particularly in Classic. 

But the moment you take a second to stare at how Classic dungeons are designed, you start to see the cracks form. Uldaman, for instance, has a level range of 41-51 in my dungeon finder. items.title: Influential Warhammer miniature designer Aly Morrison has died
items.summary:
Miniature designer and artist Aly Morrison has died, as confirmed by Trish Carden Miniatures and Design on Facebook . Carden, Morrison's ex-wife and former partner in Marauder Miniatures, posted that, "Mharaid and I are heartbroken to announce the passing of Aly Morrison, a very much loved father, veteran wargames miniatures designer and friend to many around the tabletop and the world. Aly passed unexpectedly but peacefully this Wednesday, and will be sorely missed."

Aly Morrison began sculpting for Citadel in 1983 as a freelancer before joining the studio full-time in 1986. He and Trish were then made stewards of Games Workshop's imprint Marauder Miniatures in 1988, where they had free reign to create quirky and characterful figures like the mohawked dwarf trollslayers and the giant with a whaler's beard and a booze barrel strapped to his waist that became archetypal parts of Warhammer.

Morrison also crafted the first miniatures for Blood Bowl players and drew the tokens to represent them in the board game's first edition. During his time at Games Workshop every faction from dark elves to space marines eventually benefited from his touch.

He's also well-regarded as a painter, and his reliance on a dark wash with a hint of purple in it jokingly known as "Aly's Brown Liquid" was legendary. He continued working on the recipe over the years, with a recent iteration described on his blog in 2020 if you want to whip some up yourself.

Though Marauder was eventually folded back into Citadel, Morrison continued at Games Workshop until his retirement earlier this year. The…

items.title: Are you more of an ambient music enjoyer or theatrical atmosphere appreciator?

When World of Warcraft: Forever's beta first launched, I lamented its long stretches of silence and penchant for ambience over theatrics. I still sort of stand by that, but after spending more time in Azeroth (and discovering the loop music setting) I've a new-found appreciation for both WoW's soundtrack and ambient music as a whole.

It's also got me thinking about what makes a soundtrack ambient versus something more melodic. I'm chronically Final Fantasy 14-brained, where just about everything has a grand thematic soundtrack to it—the jauntiness of the Gold Saucer, the soothing Middle-earthness of Gridania's outer Shroud zones, the grand organs of Ishgard's bitterly cold landscape. You can't escape composer Masayoshi Soken's penchant for leifmotifs. He will turn anything into an orchestral spectacle.

I'm a big JRPG fan in general, a genre I think is the absolute master of thematic soundtracks. But I also think fondly of games I've played over the years that are a little more pared down, their soundtracks there for a little atmosphere rather than actively driving the narrative. Minecraft's OST is a masterclass in ambience, and is in regular rotation across my videogame-themed Spotify playlists. I also have a huge soft spot for the soundtrack behind Mirror's Edge—one which settles in this almost otherworldly ambiance, only ramping up when Faith is in a perilous situation.

But what about you? Do you prefer the more subtle nuances that an atmospheric soundtrack has to offer? Or do you like your videogame music loud, in your face, and full of dramatics? Be sure to leave a…

While details are scarce in the teaser, some brief footage is shown where you can see what he's talking about: a Blitzcrank player selects what looks like a character-specific mastery tree labeled "God Hand," and it cuts to him beating up an enemy in melee. Other champions are shown using abilities in ways they currently can't—Vayne, for instance, dashes through a wall.

An updated art style is also shown off, including new character models for all sorts of champions as well as bosses like Baron Nashor and the Elder Dragon. It looks much more in line with the art style of Wild Rift, League of Legends' mobile port-slash-spinoff with high-detail character models.

Player reactions are, as you might expect with an update that promises to be so comprehensive, all over the map. 

"Am I the only one who thinks this looks like a mobile game," said Reddit user lukesherboiii in a thread sharing the trailer.

"The industry at large obviously saw a lot of success at that time, but we did as well, and we went from a gamer name to a household name," he said, noting it was an "unfortunate period of time for the world, but for the gaming industry, a good one, and for Jackbox, a good one as well." 

"That was kind of a leveling up for Jackbox as a company," said Bilder. "Suddenly office workers are doing happy hours and families over weekends are connecting over a game of Quiplash or something because it's what you did when you were locked down. It surprised employees at the studio to see how popular the games had become.

I decided to hop into the beta branch myself and take her for a whirl, and—yeah, those changes'll have to come. The Fool's central mechanic is her bow and arrow—she can fire an arrow/shoot card to deal damage equal to the card's base damage plus her aim. So if a shoot card deals 15 damage and she has six aim stocked, she'll deal 21. 

This is a little busted, because by default, the Fool has 6 aim already put in her bank. Her non-strike starter card, Foolish Shot, already deals a hefty 15 damage for just one energy. With aim, the first time she uses it, it deals a whopping 21 damage, which is a heck of a damage output for the Fool's first round of combat.

The saving grace here is that when a card that fires an arrow is used, that arrow becomes lodged in a target, who gains the Impale status. items.title: The Sunday Papers

Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. items.title: How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games
items.summary:

Lovecraft novella it alternately riffs on and skewers, Penguin Colony takes you to an ancient alien city of crabby cuboid geometry and helical designs – comparable at a glance to Lovecraft's "terraces of every sort of provocative disproportion", but here given strangely everyday, anachronistic-seeming labels, such as "Downtown". Later, you're shown flashes of footage of the streets of Melbourne in Australia - developer Origame Digital's base of operations, and a city built on stolen Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong Boon Wurrung land.

When I first set foot in Downtown, in the unassuming body of a Rockhopper penguin, I thought the broad idea was to satirically redefine modern settlements built by European colonisers as Lovecraftian relics, intrusions from the cosmic beyond. This irony seems most pointed in sections where you steer a group of Māori characters, journeying south to prevent an expedition of German and British Nazi occultists from resurrecting a surviving elder being they call the "one true Aryan king". Playing as one of the Māori voyagers, you witness the cyclopean city as a realm of spectral high rises and square windows, rearing out of a swamp of blood and bone.

items.summary: I often find it quite dull that the main takeaway far too many people have taken from Dark Souls , aside from thinking that the most interesting thing is its combat, is that it's all so bloomin' grimdark. I'm not saying I need sunshine and rainbows, I'd just like a vibe that's even remotely trying to be different from FromSoftware's seminal work. And so! I am quite pleased to discover MycoRelic, a Soulslike that pits you as a robot that covers its body in mushroom parts that offer elemental powers.
items.t: Cover your robot body in magical fungus aplenty and galavant across a mystical, Soulslike world in MycoRelic, now out in 1.0
